publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Education in Radar and Sonar

articleTitle: Sonars from the 1960s through to the 1990s
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Education in Radar and Sonar
abstract: The author has reviewed his own involvement in sonar design and research from the mid 1960s through to the present time. This experience has been very rewarding and has involved the author in a wide range of skills which are relevant to the designers of today, and more particularly those of the future.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A multidisciplinary approach to education in radar
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Education in Radar and Sonar
abstract: The author presents a description of the thinking behind the radar elements of an M.Sc. course offered at University College London in Microwaves and Optoelectronics. Consideration is given to the syllabus (both of the course as a whole and of the explicitly 'radar' part), the method of teaching, method of assessment, and availability and suitability of textbooks.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Education in Radar and Sonar
abstract: Bournemouth Polytechnic via the Electronics Industrial Unit run two sonar courses as part of their continuing education programme for industrial clients. The first course is run over two days and provides a basic introduction to sonar. The second more advanced course currently runs over five days, and is intended for some people who already have a basic background in sonar systems.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Collaboration in CPD between industry and academia-a consortium approach
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Education in Radar and Sonar
abstract: In seeking to harness the wealth of expertise in higher education with the size and strength of GEC a consortium of higher educational institutions with the GEC companies has been formed. Through the consortium, accredited post-graduate level of study is available on a modular basis. Modules are typically one week residential courses with pre-reading and post-course assessment or they can also be distance learning packs. The universities and polytechnics have agreed to accept each other's teaching, and so it is possible, to a certain extent, to mix modules from different establishments and to mix technical modules with personal or management development modules.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Changing industrial requirements for further education in radar
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Education in Radar and Sonar
abstract: The authors review the Bosworth M.Sc. course introduced in the 1970s and recommend a somewhat similar scheme to be spread over four or five years, minimising the periods of University tuition by means of tutorial remote learning.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: What do young radar engineers find difficult?
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Education in Radar and Sonar
abstract: The authors recognize a number of obstacles to effective understanding, some of them associated with learning any new subject, some caused by the way material is presented, some caused by inadequate background, some intrinsic to the subject, and some because of genuine difficulty of the concepts. Objectives regarded as important in the structuring of knowledge and concepts are set out.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Marine radar courses in the UK
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Education in Radar and Sonar
abstract: Technological developments increasingly have threatened a need for change in the process and product of these courses. These changes in technology coupled with government initiatives on National Vocational Qualifications have resulted in rethinking of the expected competences, course content, level, and capacity in provision.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Radar teaching at RMCS (Cranfield): undergraduate and short vocational courses
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Education in Radar and Sonar
abstract: The authors outlines a number of aspects of radar theory that seem to be equally appropriate to the apparently different needs of two groups. The undergraduates are spared the details of implementation and endless applications (in favour of a narrower but more analytical approach matched to their complementary studies) whereas for the vocational students adequate coverage of the spectrum of implementations and applications (including a significant Electronic Warfare element) is essential. Syllabi for these two courses are presented.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Experiences with international post-experience courses in sonar
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Education in Radar and Sonar
abstract: The authors have been involved in two international courses, in Sweden and Italy, organised by CEI-Europe/Elsevier. This paper describes the aims of the courses and how they are run, and discusses the part that this type of course will play in the future of higher education and continuing education for industry.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>
